newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Union backs BA cabin crew strikes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Union backs BA cabin crew strikes.

text.p: Holidaymakers looked set for a summer of discontent on Tuesday as trade union bosses gave the go-ahead to a series of 72-hour strikes by British Airways Plc cabin crew, after efforts to revive negotiations between the two sides failed.
The decision to press ahead with BA cabin crew strike action was taken by Bill Morris, general secretary of the Transport & General Workers Union (T&G) -- the union leading the dispute talks.

Morris said in a statement, "Since BA have turned a deaf ear to common sense, the union is left with no choice but to authorise the action requested by BA employees. Strike action will therefore be taken next week after the required period of seven days notice has elapsed."
A T&G spokesman told Reuters "There will be a series of 72-hour strikes." The strikes are most likely to start next Wednesday.
BA said it was in the process of drawing up a statement. The decision to proceed with cabin crew strike action was taken after unions failed to re-open talks with BA.
The strike also marks the start of the first serious industrial relations dispute since the new Labour government was elected on May 1.
The T&G said it would still welcome peace moves by BA, but a spokesman said so far "BA is sticking to its position of only talking to ground staff (over a separate dispute)."
He said this approach sealed the decision by T&G general secretary Morris to give his backing to a cabin crew strike.
Three quarters of BA's cabin crew were balloted by the T&G last week over whether to take strike action: 73 percent of those balloted said 'yes'.
The decision to press ahead with a spate of 72 hour stoppages was taken after BA chief executive Robert Ayling reiterated on Monday his hard stand against cabin crew staff last night.

Ayling said he would not enter talks until cabin crew renounced their "militancy". But he was prepared to talk to ground staff who are threatening to strike over a decision to sell of BA's catering unit. Of the ground staff who voted, 62 percent backed the strike ballot.
The T&G rebuffed the divisive approach and spent Tuesday putting more pressure on BA to hold talks with unions on both fronts.
Cabin crew are striking over a pay restructuring package, which is part of BA's wider commitment to axe one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) in costs by the year 2000.
The dispute involving ground staff -- which also backed strike action in a separate ballot on Monday -- is linked to the sale of BA's catering unit which cover 1,200 jobs.

Ground staff met earlier on Tuesday to decide whether they would follow cabin crew colleagues down the path of confrontation. If they decide to follow BA faces a momentous problem on ground and in the air.
Analysts warned the cost of strike will be onerous on BA profitability unless a last-ditch reprieve is gained.
"A strike would make a massive difference to BA -- financially in the short term as well as hurting it long term," said Chris Avery, analyst at Paribas earlier this week.
Industry observers pointed out that just the threat of a BA pilots' strike last year wiped more than 10 million pounds off group profits as passengers switched to other airlines.
BA's services from both Heathrow -- Europe's busiest airport -- and Gatwick will be hit.

The airline has already put its operations on red alert by retraining managers to take on extra roles, taken on extra security and set aside resources for taxis, coaches and hotels for strike breakers to break the picket lines.
It has warned potential strikers that they face the sack or legal action at worst and loss of promotion and benefits at worst, triggering union accusations of "intimidation and terrorism."

Such was the determination of BA's Ayling to face down the union threat that he cancelled his trip to witness the handover of Hong Kong on Monday, warning BA would not bow down to "1970s style trade unionism."
